He has just risen from his knees: his hands are still raised and spread toward heaven as he turns to bless the congregation. He faces east, toward the viewer, in a three-quarter view, the early morning sun on his face. He fills the lower two-thirds of the frame, seen from slightly below, from the knees up. answers.question: What did he carry?
answers.answer: 'Took the doors of the gate of the city, and the two posts, and went away with them, bar and all, and put them upon his shoulders, and carried them up to the top of an hill that is before Hebron' (Judg 16:3). Doors (two leaves), the two doorposts and the bar; no lintel. Iron Age gate doors were two leaves of planks with cross-battens, often plated or studded with metal, turning on pivot posts set in socket stones at the threshold, and shut by a wooden bar into the jambs; the gate passage was about 3-4 m wide (Dan, Lachish, Megiddo, Gezer). The first picture drew a frame like an upside-down doorway with doors hanging from it; now he carries the two leaves flat across his shoulders with the posts and bar lashed on.
sources: Z. Herzog, Das Stadttor in Israel und in den Nachbarländern (1986)
Neh 3:3, 6 (doors, locks and bars of a gate)
Ps 107:16 (gates of brass, bars of iron)

answers.question: When?
answers.answer: He 'lay till midnight, and arose at midnight' (16:3); how long the climb took is not said. The first picture had a sunset; now it is the end of the night, dawn ahead in the east. 'Before Hebron' (Heb. 'al-penei, facing Hebron) is unlocated: Hebron is about 60 km from Gaza and some 900 m higher; tradition points also to the hill el-Muntar east of Gaza. The text is silent which.

after.changes: The gate redrawn as the two plank doors with their pivot posts, the two doorposts and the bar across his shoulders, no frame; the end of the night with dawn ahead; same face, braids and tunic.

answers.question: Was the boat on the shore?
answers.answer: No. Mark 4:1: 'he entered into a ship, and sat in the sea; and the whole multitude was by the sea on the land'; Matt 13:2: 'he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore'; Luke 5:3: he asked Simon 'that he would thrust out a little from the land. And he sat down, and taught the people out of the ship'. The boat was afloat a little way out, he sat in it, the crowd was on land.

answers.question: Stones or sand on that shore?
answers.answer: The Gospels say only 'shore' (Gk aigialos, Matt 13:2) and 'land'. Geology: the north-west shore from Tabgha to Capernaum lies on the basalt of the Korazim plateau; its beaches are dark basalt pebbles and cobbles mixed with small pale freshwater shells, with grass and basalt boulders on the slope above. Capernaum itself is built of basalt. Sand is rare on that stretch. The cove between Tabgha and Capernaum ('Bay of Parables') is a natural sloping theatre where a voice from a boat carries to a large crowd on the shore (Crisler 1976). So the stones are right; they are now basalt pebbles and cobbles at the waterline rather than large rocks.
sources: B. C. Crisler, 'The Acoustics and Crowd Capacity of Natural Theaters in Palestine', Biblical Archaeologist 39.4 (1976) 128-141
V. Corbo, Cafarnao I (Jerusalem 1975): basalt construction of Capernaum
S. Wachsmann, The Sea of Galilee Boat (1995): the 1st-century boat from Ginosar, 8.2 x 2.3 m, cedar and oak, mast and oars

answers.question: Were the sacks brought in?
answers.answer: The text does not bring them in. The sacks were opened on the road outside the city (Gen 44:11-12); then 'they rent their clothes, and laded every man his ass, and returned to the city' (44:13); 'Judah and his brethren came to Joseph's house' (44:14). On the first visit the steward fed their asses at the house (43:24), so the animals and loads were in the house's yard, not in the hall where Joseph received them. The sacks are taken out of the picture.

answers.question: Was it a royal palace, and in a courtyard?
answers.answer: Neither. The plea was in 'Joseph's house' (Gen 44:14; also 43:16-17, 26), his own residence, not Pharaoh's palace. A high Egyptian official's house (the Amarna villas are the best-known plans) stood in a walled compound with a court, but the master received visitors in the roofed central hall with wooden columns, lit by small windows high under the roof. The new picture is set in such a hall. One detail from the text is added: their clothes were torn (44:13).
sources: B. Kemp, The City of Akhenaten and Nefertiti: Amarna and Its People (2012), ch. on houses
H. Frankfort and J. D. S. Pendlebury, The City of Akhenaten II (1933): the house of the vizier Nakht

after.changes: Set in the roofed hall of Joseph's house, no sacks; Judah's tunic torn at the neck (44:13); Joseph in a wig, not a royal head-cloth; same face and wrap.

answers.answer: Twelve stones, one for each tribe (1 Kgs 18:31-32), and a trench 'as great as would contain two measures of seed' (18:32): two seahs, read either as a volume (about 15-25 litres) or, by the Mishnaic idiom bet se'atayim, as the area sown with two seahs (about 5,000 square cubits). Either way a sizeable trench, which needs an altar of large stones; twelve stones can only make a big altar if they are boulders. The fire consumed 'the stones, and the dust' too (18:38).

answers.question: Did everyone fall at once?
answers.answer: 18:39: 'when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces' - all of them, but a picture of the instant the fire falls can show some already down and others still rising to it. Done so.

answers.question: The prophets of Baal
answers.answer: They had their own altar with their bullock on wood and no fire (18:23, 25-26), 'leaped upon the altar' (18:26) and 'cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them' (18:28), from noon until the evening offering (18:29). The text does not say they tore their clothes. They are now in the picture, small in the middle distance by their unlit altar, exhausted, knives in hand; Elijah stays the focus. Their wounds are not drawn: Codex's image tool refused the first request because it showed self-inflicted wounds.

after.changes: Same Elijah, pose, sky and fire; the altar made of twelve huge boulders, much bigger; the crowd reacting at different moments; the prophets of Baal small in the distance by their own altar.

answers.question: What was torn?
answers.answer: Ahijah 'had clad himself with a new garment; and they two were alone in the field: And Ahijah caught the new garment that was on him, and rent it in twelve pieces: And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces' (1 Kgs 11:29-31). Heb. salmah, the outer wrap, the same garment as simlah: a large rectangle of woollen cloth worn by day and slept in by night (Exod 22:26-27; Deut 22:17). Mantles from the Cave of Letters (2nd c. AD, the best preserved from the land) are about 1.5 x 2.5-3 m. Twelve pieces of such a cloth are each about the size of a large towel. The pieces are now drawn large, new and clean, all with parts of the same woven bands, ten folded in Jeroboam's arms and two in Ahijah's hands.
sources: Y. Yadin, The Finds from the Bar Kokhba Period in the Cave of Letters (1963): mantles

after.changes: The torn garment redrawn as twelve large pieces of one new cream mantle with matching red and indigo bands; the same two men and setting.

answers.question: What was the mantle?
answers.answer: 'The mantle of Elijah that fell from him' (2 Kgs 2:13-14), Heb. 'adderet: a wide cloak, the prophet's garment, 'a rough garment' ('adderet se'ar, garment of hair) in Zech 13:4; Elijah was 'an hairy man' (2 Kgs 1:8), read by many as 'a man with a garment of hair'. So a large cloak of coarse woven goat hair, the same dark cloth as in Elijah's approved picture. Elijah 'wrapped it together' before striking (2:8); Elisha simply 'took the mantle ... and smote the waters' (2:14). Drawn now as a cloak held folded in both hands, partly unfolding.
sources: 1 Kgs 19:19 (the same mantle cast on Elisha)

answers.question: What did the river do?
answers.answer: 'They parted hither and thither: and Elisha went over' (2:14); for Elijah 'they two went over on dry ground' (2:8). The text gives no walls of water. The Jordan near Jericho winds through its own thicket (the zor, 'the swelling of Jordan', Jer 12:5) between grey marl badlands; before modern diversion it was some 20-30 m wide here, with Jericho's oasis about 8 km to the west. The new picture keeps the river narrow and muddy, the water held back low upstream and draining away downstream, a strip of wet bed between.

answers.question: What were the altars like?
answers.answer: 'Build me here seven altars, and prepare me here seven oxen and seven rams. And Balak did as Balaam had spoken; and Balak and Balaam offered on every altar a bullock and a ram' (Num 23:1-2; again 23:14, 29-30). Balak then 'stood by his burnt sacrifice, he, and all the princes of Moab' (23:6). The text gives no build; an altar that burns a whole bullock and a ram is a large one. Archaeology of the region: altars of unhewn stone packed with earth, square and about waist to chest high (the Arad sanctuary altar, about 2.4 m square; the Mount Ebal structure; Exod 20:24-25 for earth and unhewn stone). The first picture made small stone boxes with coals; now seven large altars with the offerings burning, Balak and his princes beside them. The Deir Alla plaster text (c. 800 BC) names 'Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods', outside the Bible.
sources: Z. Herzog, 'The Arad Fortresses', in Arad (1997)
J. Hoftijzer and G. van der Kooij, Aramaic Texts from Deir 'Alla (1976)

after.owner: Interesting, but the scene is very wrong in scale and in how it happened. Re-read Num 22:41-23:30 and choose one moment with the right scale.

answers.question: What happened, in order?
answers.answer: Three times the same pattern, each at a new height: the high places of Baal, whence 'he might see the utmost part of the people' (22:41); the field of Zophim on top of Pisgah, where 'thou shalt see but the utmost part of them, and shalt not see them all' (23:13-14); the top of Peor 'that looketh toward Jeshimon' (23:28). Each time seven altars were built and a bullock and a ram offered on every one (23:1-2, 14, 29-30); Balak stayed 'by his burnt offering' with the princes of Moab (23:6, 17) while Balaam went apart to 'an high place' to meet God (23:3, 15), then came back and 'took up his parable' (23:7, 18). Only at Peor did he see 'Israel abiding in his tents according to their tribes' (24:2).

answers.question: Which moment, and at what scale?
answers.answer: The first oracle (23:6-7): Balaam back from the height before Balak, who stands by his burnt offering with all the princes, at Bamoth-baal. The heights of the Moabite plateau above the plains of Moab (Mount Nebo/Pisgah about 700-800 m above sea level, the plains near the Jordan about 300-350 m below it) lie some 10-15 km from the camp at Abel-shittim, so the camp is drawn small and distant, only its edge in view. Bamoth-baal is not located for certain (proposed near Mount Nebo, cf. Josh 13:17).
sources: Y. Aharoni, The Land of the Bible (1979) on the plains of Moab

after.changes: Redrawn with true scale at one moment (Num 23:6-7): seven waist-high altars, Balak and the princes life-size by the burnt offering, Balaam returning and speaking, the camp far off and small.

answers.question: What were the gates of a Philistine city like?
answers.answer: Gaza's Iron Age levels lie under the old city (Tell Harube) and have hardly been dug (a sounding by W. J. Phythian-Adams in 1922), so its gate is unknown. Comparable gates: the six-chambered gates of Ashdod (Area M, Iron IIA), Gezer, Megiddo and Hazor (10th-9th c.), the gates of Tel Miqne-Ekron, Lachish and Dan. Their passages are about 4 m wide (roughly 4.1-4.3 m at Gezer, Megiddo and Hazor), closed by two wooden door leaves that turned on pivot posts in socket stones at either side of the threshold, met against a central stop, and were locked by a wooden bar slid into recesses in the jambs (Judg 16:3; Deut 3:5; Neh 3:3, 6; 1 Kgs 4:13 'great cities with walls and brasen bars'). So each leaf was about 2 m wide; their height is nowhere preserved, and 3-4 m is a reasonable estimate from the passage proportions. Wooden gate doors were often strapped or plated with bronze (the Balawat gates of Shalmaneser III, 9th c., British Museum; Ps 107:16 'gates of brass'). The first redraw's load was roughly right in kind but not in scale.
sources: Z. Herzog, Das Stadttor in Israel und in den Nachbarländern (1986); Herzog, 'Gate, City', ABD II (1992)
M. Dothan and Y. Porath, Ashdod IV (1982): the Area M gate
W. G. Dever et al., Gezer IV (1986) / 'Solomonic gates' at Gezer, Megiddo, Hazor (Yadin 1958)
T. Dothan and S. Gitin, Tel Miqne-Ekron excavation reports

answers.question: Was Samson a giant?
answers.answer: The text never describes his size. The Philistines had to ask Delilah 'wherein his great strength lieth' (16:5), so it was not visible in his build; he says that shaven he would 'be like any other man' (16:17); his feats come when 'the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him' (14:6, 19; 15:14). So an ordinary strong man is right. Carrying some 1-2 tonnes of gate up a hill is what the text presents as more than human strength; the picture keeps a normal man under a credibly huge load.

Guards at the entrance: the keepers of the door were priests (2 Kgs 23:4; 12:9); armed men stand in the temple only at Joash's crowning (2 Kgs 11); removed. Walls: the inner court wall was three courses of hewn stone and a course of cedar beams (1 Kgs 6:36), low. Second notes (2026-11-18): redrawn on the king's stand before the altar, the people further off. Where the king stood: 'al ha-'ammud' (2 Kgs 23:3; 11:14 'as the manner was') is rendered by the Chronicler 'al 'omdo', 'on his stand / in his place' (2 Chr 34:31; the same word for the priests' posts, 2 Chr 30:16; 35:10), and for Joash 'on his stand at the entrance' (2 Chr 23:13): a fixed royal standing-place, most consistently a raised platform in the court before the altar like Solomon's (2 Chr 6:13), not the porch pillars, whose ground between porch and altar was the priests' (Joel 2:17; 2 Chr 26:16-20). Gold: inside overlaid (1 Kgs 6:20-22, 30; porch 2 Chr 3:4), doors gold-covered (6:32, 35), outside stone; Hezekiah stripped the doors and doorposts (2 Kgs 18:16); nothing says Josiah re-covered them (his repairs paid carpenters and masons, 2 Kgs 22:5-6).

answers.question: How to show 'parted hither and thither' credibly
answers.answer: 2 Kgs 2:14 says only that the waters 'parted hither and thither' and that Elisha went over; 2:8 has Elijah and Elisha cross 'on dry ground'. The same river near the same place has one fuller description: when Israel crossed 'right against Jericho', 'the waters which came down from above stood and rose up upon an heap very far from the city Adam ... and those that came down toward the sea of the plain ... failed, and were cut off' (Josh 3:16). The picture follows that pattern, which the owner also asked for: the river stopped and heaped upstream, the downstream bed drained. Two things are staging, not text: 2 Kings does not describe the parting this way (it is an analogy with Joshua 3), and in Joshua 3 the heap stood far upstream at Adam, while the picture brings it into view in the middle distance at about a man's height. The deep channel with high marl banks and the thicket (Jer 12:5 'the swelling of Jordan') is the lower Jordan's real form.

In the middle distance, upstream, the river is stopped: the brown water stands heaped up across the whole channel from bank to bank, a smooth, rounded mass about as high as a man, with the strong current visibly pressing and churning behind it and the full river beyond running high between its banks (as the Jordan stood in a heap at the crossing of Joshua 3:16). In the foreground, downstream, the channel is drained: a bare bed of wet mud, gravel and stones with a few shallow puddles, the dark water-marks high on both banks showing how deep the river ran. Elisha walks across this dry bed from one bank toward the other, from left to right, in the foreground, his face turned three-quarters to the viewer, steady and resolved. No other people; the grey marl hills beyond the banks; late afternoon light. Not a marsh, not a shallow stream, not a red-sea wall of glassy water. Anatomy must be correct: every person has two arms, two hands with five fingers and two legs. No text, letters or inscriptions anywhere in the image; no halo; no modern objects; Near Eastern features and colouring, not European. Correction to the previous try, in which he looked away over his shoulder: keep that riverbed, banks, heaped water and mantle, but Elisha looks where he is going, ahead toward the far bank, his face turned three-quarters toward the viewer, calm and resolved, eyes not glancing sideways or back. He walks across the bed, not along it.

Portrait orientation, 2:3. Elisha at the Jordan, the moment before he strikes the water with Elijah's mantle and cries 'Where is the LORD God of Elijah?' (2 Kings 2:13-14). He is the same man as in the attached picture: keep his face, bald head, full dark beard, olive-brown skin and build. He wears an undyed wool tunic to the knee, torn open from the neck down the chest where he rent his clothes in grief (2 Kings 2:12), a leather belt and sandals. Elijah's mantle is a big rectangular cloak of thick, coarse, dark brown goat-hair cloth, about two metres long and one and a half wide, with a plain woven border and a tassel at each corner: plainly a garment, not a fleece, rope, net or bundle. He stands alone at the water's edge on the east bank, on wet mud among reeds, seen from a little to the side and in front, at three-quarter length, large in the picture, his face turned toward the river and three-quarters toward the viewer, lit and readable, full of grief and resolve. He holds the mantle high above his head in both hands, raised to strike, its broad length unfolding and hanging down behind him, a corner tassel swinging. The real lower Jordan opposite Jericho in late spring flood (Joshua 3:15): a single brown, fast river some twenty-five metres wide, its current streaked with foam and eddies, flowing from left to right, running full between low banks of mud fringed with reeds, tall cane, willows and tamarisks: the green thicket of the floodplain. Beyond the far bank the green thicket gives way to the bare grey-white marl badlands of the valley terraces, eroded into pale crumbling hills. The river beside and before him is still flowing in full, unbroken: nothing has parted yet. On the far, western side, beyond the badlands, the green oasis of Jericho with palms and, far off and tiny on a rise, a small group of men watching from afar (the sons of the prophets, 2 Kings 2:7); the hills of Judea on the horizon. Clear afternoon light. The river must read at once as a big, deep, fast river, not a marsh. Anatomy must be correct: every person has two arms, two hands with five fingers and two legs. No text, letters or inscriptions anywhere in the image; no halo; no modern objects; Near Eastern features and colouring, not European. Correction to a first try in which he looked away from the river: his head is turned toward the river and lifted a little, as he cries out 'Where is the LORD God of Elijah?', his mouth slightly open, his face in clear three-quarter view toward the viewer and the water; the camera a little closer, so that his head is larger in the picture, while the river, its far bank and the badlands still fill the right side.

after.owner: Still unclear where he is and what is happening; the sides do not read as water at all. Rethink the whole scene from scratch; perhaps on the bank of a big river.

answers.question: Where did it happen?
answers.answer: At the Jordan opposite Jericho. Elijah and Elisha went from Jericho to the Jordan (2 Kgs 2:4-6); 'fifty men of the sons of the prophets went, and stood to view afar off: and they two stood by Jordan' (2:7); they crossed east on dry ground (2:8), Elijah was taken up beyond the river, and Elisha 'went back, and stood by the bank of Jordan' (2:13), so on the east bank, struck the water and went over west; 'the sons of the prophets which were to view at Jericho saw him' (2:15). The place is near where Israel crossed 'right against Jericho' (Josh 3:16).

answers.question: What does the place look like?
answers.answer: The lower Jordan winds in its own narrow floodplain, the Zor, a green thicket of tamarisk, willow and cane ('the swelling of Jordan', Jer 12:5), cut below the bare grey-white marl terraces of the valley (the Qattara badlands); Jericho's oasis lies some 8 km to the west under the Judean hills, the Moab plateau rises to the east. Before modern diversion the river here was about 20-30 m wide, brown and fast, and 'Jordan overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest' (Josh 3:15).
sources: D. Baly, The Geography of the Bible (1974)

answers.question: Which moment, and why
answers.answer: Three were weighed: (a) Elisha on the east bank raising the mantle to strike, the river still flowing; (b) just after the strike, the water divided; (c) Elisha come up on the west bank wearing the mantle, the sons of the prophets bowing far off. Two were drawn, (a) and (c). (a) was kept: it says at once where he is (on the bank of a big, fast, deep river) and what is happening (he lifts Elijah's cloak against the water), it shows the mantle open at full size as a garment, and it draws nothing the text does not describe; (b) needs a picture of the parting, which 2 Kings gives no shape for and which failed three times; (c) read well but as a quiet standing portrait the river is only background and the story is less clear. His own clothes are torn, as the text says he rent them (2:12).

after.label: Ploughing at Abel-meholah when Elijah casts his mantle upon him (1 Kgs 19:19)
after.basis: 1 Kgs 19:16, 19-21: Elisha son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah, 'plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him'; afterwards he slew a yoke of oxen and boiled their flesh 'with the instruments of the oxen'. Archaeology: the Iron Age plough was an ard, a wooden body with a single handle and an iron point (iron ploughpoints from Iron Age sites; 1 Sam 13:20-21 'share', 'coulter', 'goads'), drawn by a pair of oxen under a wooden neck yoke; small humpless Levantine cattle. Abel-meholah is in the Jordan valley south of Beth-shean (often placed at Tel Abu Sus or Tell el-Hilu). Twelve pairs ploughing one behind another is the usual reading; the picture shows a line of teams ahead, not counted.

He stands alone at the water's edge on the east bank, on wet mud among reeds, seen from a little to the side and in front, at three-quarter length, large in the picture, his face turned toward the river and three-quarters toward the viewer, lit and readable, full of grief and resolve. He holds the mantle high above his head in both hands, raised to strike, its broad length unfolding and hanging down behind him, a corner tassel swinging. The real lower Jordan opposite Jericho in late spring flood (Joshua 3:15): a single brown, fast river some twenty-five metres wide, its current streaked with foam and eddies, flowing from left to right, running full between low banks of mud fringed with reeds, tall cane, willows and tamarisks: the green thicket of the floodplain. Beyond the far bank the green thicket gives way to the bare grey-white marl badlands of the valley terraces, eroded into pale crumbling hills. The river beside and before him is still flowing in full, unbroken: nothing has parted yet. On the far, western side, beyond the badlands, the green oasis of Jericho with palms and, far off and tiny on a rise, a small group of men watching from afar (the sons of the prophets, 2 Kings 2:7); the hills of Judea on the horizon. answers.answer: 2 Kgs 2:15: 'they came to meet him, and bowed themselves to the ground before him'. Left out of option A at the owner's word; the text is not contradicted by leaving them out of the frame.

answers.question: Why the spring of Jericho for the third option
answers.answer: Of the candidates it is the most literal and the most legible in one picture: one man, one act (salt cast from a new bowl into a spring, 2 Kgs 2:19-22), a known place (the spring at the foot of Tell es-Sultan), right after the Jordan crossing, so the mantle belongs in it, and nothing visionary. Naaman hardly shows Elisha (he sends a messenger, 5:10); the floating axe head (6:1-7) is another Jordan scene, which has been hard to make readable; Dothan's horses and chariots of fire are seen when the servant's eyes are opened (6:17), close to a vision; the Shunammite's son (4:32-37) puts a dead child and Elisha lying on him at the centre, which is hard to show with dignity in a portrait.
